children: Chicago Board of Trade soybean and grain futures slumped on Thursday as traders waited to see whether a highly anticipated US-China summit would produce agricultural trade deals.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on Wednesday after talks with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng that they had agreed to extend until January 10 an agreement pausing a trade war that saw mutual tariffs top 100%.

However, traders were hoping for China to announce it would buy specific amounts of US crops or remove a 10% tariff on imports of US soybeans in conjunction with a meeting between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Washington.
"We have not gotten into the meat of it," said Ted Seifried, chief market strategist for Zaner Ag Hedge. "That is what the market is waiting for. The market is getting a little impatient."

Traders were eager to learn details of potential deals after the White House ‌said in May that Beijing committed to purchasing at least $17 billion of US agricultural ​products in 2026, 2027 and 2028.
"We haven't really seen evidence that China is following through on that," Seifried said.
Grain markets came under additional pressure as the dollar hit a fresh two-month high, making US agricultural goods look more expensive to importers.

Renewed diplomatic efforts to end the Ukraine war also kept traders' attention on the outlook for Black Sea grain exports. Turkey said it had stepped up efforts to re-establish the Black Sea grain corridor and received a positive response from Ukraine.
Traders hope for a recovery in cargo movements that are at a near standstill in the Black Sea due to heavy attacks on ships and port infrastructure by Russia and Ukraine.
